mcqs.question: What problem does a circuit breaker primarily protect against?
options: It makes the failing downstream dependency recover faster
It protects the caller from wasting threads and connections on requests to a dependency that's already failing
It automatically retries failed requests until they succeed
It caches responses so the dependency is never called twice for the same input
mcqs.explanation: A circuit breaker stops the caller from repeatedly spending resources on calls likely to fail — it doesn't speed up the dependency's own recovery, isn't a retry mechanism, and isn't a cache; those are separate concerns entirely.

mcqs.question: In the circuit breaker state machine, how does the breaker get from Open back to Closed?
options: Directly, once the cooldown timer elapses
It never returns to Closed once opened; a new breaker instance must be created
Only by moving through Half-Open first and having trial requests succeed
Automatically, based on the dependency's own health-check endpoint
mcqs.explanation: There's no direct Open-to-Closed transition — the cooldown timer only moves the breaker to Half-Open, and it's the trial requests succeeding there that closes it. The breaker doesn't rely on an external health-check endpoint, and it certainly can recover without recreating the instance.

mcqs.question: A downstream service is having a genuine, sustained outage lasting several minutes. Which mechanism alone is insufficient, and why?
options: Plain retries alone, because they'll keep resending requests to a dependency that's still down, adding more load to an already-struggling service
A circuit breaker alone, because it never allows any requests through again once tripped
Both are equally sufficient on their own for any outage duration
Neither mechanism is relevant to a sustained outage, only to single dropped packets
mcqs.explanation: Retries assume a transient blip; against a sustained outage, they just keep amplifying load on a service that's already failing. A circuit breaker does allow requests through again via half-open probing, so it isn't a one-way lock, and both mechanisms are in fact relevant here — retries alone is the one that's insufficient.

mcqs.question: A circuit breaker keeps flipping between open and closed every few seconds during an incident. What does this usually indicate?
options: The breaker is working exactly as designed and needs no changes
The failure threshold is too lenient and should be raised further
The trip threshold is too sensitive or the cooldown too short, so probes hit the dependency before it can genuinely recover
The dependency has fully recovered and the breaker should be removed
mcqs.explanation: Rapid flapping usually means the breaker reacts to normal noise (threshold too sensitive) or re-probes too soon (cooldown too short), each probe adding load right when the dependency is most fragile. This isn't healthy operation, raising the threshold further wouldn't necessarily fix cooldown timing, and flapping is itself evidence the dependency hasn't stably recovered.
